title: Breaking Two Hours: The Science Behind the Marathon's Greatest Barrier
summary: When Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in 2019, he became the first human to run a marathon in under two hours. It was one of sport's greatest achievements — and it tells us something profound about the limits of human endurance.
content:
For decades, the two-hour marathon was athletics' equivalent of the four-minute mile — a barrier that seemed to define the outer limit of human capability. Physiologists calculated that sustaining the pace required (approximately 2:50 per kilometre for 42.195 kilometres) demanded an oxygen consumption rate that was theoretically at the edge of what a human body could maintain.

Then Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna on October 12, 2019, and the barrier fell.

The Kipchoge Factor

Eliud Kipchoge is not just the greatest marathon runner in history — he is one of the greatest endurance athletes who has ever lived. His VO2 max (a measure of oxygen processing capacity) is extraordinary. His running economy — the efficiency with which he converts oxygen into forward motion — is better than any tested runner. And his mental approach to the marathon, described by coaches as uniquely calm and controlled, allows him to run at the edge of his physiological limits without the anxiety that causes other runners to slow.

But the Vienna attempt — the INEOS 1:59 Challenge — was not just about Kipchoge. It was a carefully engineered assault on the barrier, with every variable optimised.

The Technology

The Nike Vaporfly shoes worn by Kipchoge in Vienna contained a carbon fibre plate and a highly responsive foam that returned energy with each foot strike. Studies suggested they improved running economy by 4% — a staggering advantage in a sport where margins of improvement are measured in fractions of a percent.

The course in Vienna was chosen for its flat profile and favourable weather. Pacemakers ran in a rotating V-formation designed to reduce wind resistance for Kipchoge. A laser projected the ideal pace line on the road ahead. Everything that could be controlled was controlled.

No human is limited. That was what Kipchoge said afterwards. It sounds like a motivational poster. But he had just proved it, running a distance that physiologists had said could not be run that fast, in a time that no one had run before.

What It Means for the Official Record

The Vienna run does not count as an official world record because of the pacemaking arrangements and other conditions that do not meet World Athletics rules. The official marathon world record — also held by Kipchoge, set in Berlin in 2022 at 2:01:09 — is a different kind of achievement: a race, against other competitors, under standard conditions.

But the Vienna run proved that two hours was possible. And once something has been shown to be possible, the question becomes not whether it will happen officially, but when.

The Next Barrier

With shoe technology improving, with training methods becoming more sophisticated, with the global pool of East African distance running talent continuing to produce extraordinary athletes, the official sub-two-hour marathon feels like a matter of time. The question is which athlete will be the one to do it — and whether we will be watching when they cross the line.
